options: Return isError with a transient category and isRetryable: true.
Return isError with a business-rule category and a message the agent can relay.
Return a successful result with an empty list, noting that nothing matched.
Return isError with a permission category so the agent hands off to staff.

h.stem: The order-lookup tool finds no orders for the email a customer gives. It currently returns isError, so the agent tells the customer the system is down. What should the tool return?
why: Right for timeouts that a retry would fix. Nothing failed here.
Right when a policy blocks the action. Nothing was blocked; there are just no matches.
A search that ran and found nothing succeeded; the agent can then ask for another email.
Right when access is denied. The search ran fine.

p.stem: A refund request falls outside the 90-day policy window. The tool returns “Operation failed,” and the agent retries three times before apologizing vaguely. What should the tool return?
why: Right for transient faults. A policy limit won't change on retry.
A business-rule error tells the agent not to retry, and gives it something to explain to the customer.
Right when a search finds nothing. The refund was refused.
Right when credentials don't allow the action. This is a policy decision.

options: Mark the error as transient and retryable so the agent tries again.
Return a validation error naming the field and the format it expects.
Return a business-rule error that names the policy blocking the action.
Return a permission error so the agent passes the request to staff with access.

h.stem: The shipping API times out under load about 2% of the time, and a second attempt almost always succeeds. The agent gives up after the first failure. What should the tool return on a timeout?
why: Telling the agent the failure is transient and retryable lets it try once more.
Right when the input is malformed. The input here is fine.
Right when a policy blocks the action. Nothing is blocked.
Right when access is denied. This is load, not access.

p.stem: The agent passes order numbers like “#A-1234,” but the tool expects “A1234.” The tool returns “Error,” and the agent keeps retrying with the same input. What should the tool return?
why: Right for transient faults. Retrying the same input fails the same way.
Naming the field and the expected format lets the agent fix its input.
Right when a policy blocks the action. This is an input format problem.
Right when access is denied. This is an input format problem.

options: Have the subagent retry transient failures itself and report only what it can't resolve.
Return the error to the coordinator with the query, what was tried and any partial results.
Return an empty result marked as a successful search with no matches.
Return a permission error so the coordinator stops using that source.

h.stem: A search subagent hits occasional rate-limit errors that clear within seconds. Each one goes to the coordinator, which re-plans the whole task. What fits best?
why: Handle recoverable errors where they happen, and escalate only what the subagent can't fix.
Right for failures the subagent can't recover from. These clear in seconds.
Right when the search ran and found nothing. Here the search failed.
Right when access is denied. Rate limits are temporary.

p.stem: An archive's API is down for maintenance for the next hour. After its retries fail, the subagent reports only “search failed,” and the coordinator can't decide whether to wait or use another source. What fits best?
why: Right for brief, transient errors. Retries have already failed.
With the details and partial results, the coordinator can choose a sensible alternative.
That would hide a real failure as an empty search.
Right when credentials are refused. This source will return within the hour.

options: Return a tool result with isError: true and a message saying what to fix.
Return an empty result set as a success when the query matches nothing.
Mark rate-limit failures as retryable so the client waits and tries again.
Return a JSON-RPC protocol error for a malformed request, such as an unknown tool.

h.stem: An internal MCP tool throws an exception when a developer's query returns no tickets, and Claude reports that the tracker is broken. What should the tool do?
why: Right for invalid input. The query was valid and simply matched nothing.
No matches is a valid answer, not a failure.
Right for rate limits. Nothing was limited.
Right for malformed protocol messages. The request was well formed.

p.stem: When a tool's date argument is malformed, the server returns a JSON-RPC error. Claude never sees what went wrong, so it can't correct the call. What should the tool do?
why: Under the current MCP spec, input-validation errors go back as tool results the model can read and act on.
Right when the query matches nothing. Here the input is invalid.
Right for rate limits. Here the input is invalid.
That's the current behavior, and the model never sees it.

options: Give each agent only the 4–5 tools its role needs.
Set tool_choice to "auto" so Claude can reply in text when no tool is needed.
Set tool_choice to "any" so Claude must call one of the tools.
Give the agent one narrow lookup tool from another role, not that role's full toolset.

h.stem: The support agent often only needs to answer a greeting or a simple policy question, but it's configured so that every response must call a tool, so it invents lookups. What fixes this?
why: Right when too many tools confuse selection. Here a tool call is forced when none is needed.
With "auto", Claude calls a tool only when one is needed.
That is the problem: it forces a call on every turn.
Right when a role needs one capability from another role. Here no tool is needed at all.

p.stem: The support agent has 22 tools across billing, shipping and returns, and it often picks the wrong one. What fixes this?
why: Fewer, role-specific tools make selection reliable.
Right when tool calls are forced unnecessarily. Here the problem is choice overload.
Right when output must be structured. It doesn't help choose among 22.
Right for one cross-role capability. Here the toolset is already too large.

options: Give the synthesis agent a narrow verify_fact tool for quick checks.
Send verification requests back through the coordinator to the search agent.
Remove the web-search tools from the document-analysis subagent.
Force the citation-formatting tool on the synthesis agent's final step.

h.stem: The synthesis agent often needs to confirm one date or figure. Each check goes back through the coordinator to the search agent, adding minutes per report. What fits best?
why: A scoped tool covers the common, simple check without a full round trip.
That is the slow path here. It's right for larger follow-up research.
Right when an agent strays outside its role. Here the problem is latency.
Right when the final output must follow a format. Here the problem is latency.

p.stem: Synthesis sometimes needs a deeper follow-up investigation, involving several searches. The team wants the coordinator to keep track of all research done. What fits best?
why: Right for quick single-fact checks. This is real research the coordinator should track.
Routing through the coordinator keeps it aware of all research and able to plan.
Right when an agent strays outside its role. Here the coordinator needs visibility.
Right for formatting. This is about research flow.

options: State each tool's scope in its description, and when to use the other.
Rename the tools so that each name states what the tool is for.
Add examples of the expected input format to the tool's description.
Split the generic tool into separate tools, each with one narrow purpose.

h.stem: search_web and search_docs both have the description “Searches for information.” The agent picks the wrong one about a third of the time. What fixes this?
why: The model chooses tools mainly from their descriptions; say what each covers and where each one's scope ends.
Right when names mislead. These names are already distinct; the descriptions are identical.
Right when the input is malformed. Here the wrong tool is chosen.
Right when one tool does several jobs. These are already separate.

p.stem: The agent calls search_papers with full sentences, but the tool expects keyword queries plus a year range such as “2020-2024.” What fixes this?
why: Right when tools get confused with each other. Here the right tool gets the wrong input.
Right when names mislead. The tool is chosen correctly.
Showing the expected input format in the description fixes how the tool is called.
Right when one tool does several jobs. This one does one.

options: Add the server to the project's .mcp.json and commit it.
Add the server in user scope so it's available in all of one person's projects.
Reference the token as ${GITHUB_TOKEN} in .mcp.json instead of pasting it in.
Use the maintained community GitHub server rather than building a custom one.

h.stem: The team's .mcp.json has a personal access token pasted in, so it can't be committed and each developer edits it by hand. What fixes this?
why: Right for sharing a server. The token still can't be committed.
Right for a personal server. The team still needs a shared configuration.
Environment variable expansion keeps the secret out of the file, so the configuration can be shared.
Right when a custom build duplicates an existing server. Here the issue is the secret.

p.stem: A developer wants an experimental MCP server available in every project they work on, without teammates getting it. What fits best?
why: Right for team-wide servers. This would push it on teammates.
User scope follows one person across projects and isn't shared.
Right for keeping secrets out of the file. This is about who gets the server.
Right for standard integrations. This is about where it's configured.

options: Expose the documentation catalog as MCP resources.
Build a custom MCP server for the team's in-house deployment system.
Use an existing, maintained community server for the standard integration.
Add the server to the project's .mcp.json so everyone gets it.

h.stem: The team plans to spend two weeks building an MCP server for Jira. A maintained community server already covers everything they need. What fits best?
why: Right when Claude needs to browse what content exists. Here the question is build versus reuse.
Right for in-house systems that no existing server covers. Jira is covered.
Reuse a maintained server for a standard integration; build only what's unique.
Right for sharing a server. It doesn't settle whether to build one.

p.stem: Before every task, Claude runs dozens of exploratory search calls just to find out which internal docs exist. What fits best?
why: Resources let the client see what content is available without exploratory tool calls.
Right when no server exists for an in-house system. Here Claude needs a catalog.
Right for standard integrations. Here Claude needs a catalog.
Right for sharing a server. Here Claude needs a catalog.

options: Commit the server configuration to the project's .mcp.json.
Keep the server in local scope, for this one developer and this one project.
Rewrite the MCP tool's description to say when it beats the built-ins.
Expose the read-only reference data as MCP resources rather than tools.

h.stem: The team's MCP code-search tool is more accurate than Grep for this repository, but Claude keeps using Grep. The MCP tool's description reads “Search tool.” What fixes this?
why: Right when teammates don't get the server. They have it; Claude doesn't choose it.
Right for a personal server. The problem is tool selection.
Claude picks tools by their descriptions; a vague one loses to a familiar built-in.
Right when Claude needs to browse content. This is a search tool.

p.stem: A new developer clones the repository and doesn't get the team's database MCP server, which everyone else uses. What fixes this?
why: Project scope is shared through the repository.
Right for a personal server. Here the team needs to share it.
Right when Claude won't pick the tool. Here the server isn't there at all.
Right for browsable content. Here the server isn't there at all.

options: Use Grep to search file contents for the function name.
Use Glob to find files by a name pattern such as **/*.test.ts.
Use Edit with a longer anchor that appears only once in the file.
Read the whole file and write back the full corrected version.

h.stem: An Edit fails because the target text appears in several places in the file. No surrounding text reliably picks out the right occurrence. What should Claude do?
why: Right for finding where text appears across files. Here the problem is editing one file.
Right for finding files by name. Here the problem is editing one file.
Right when a unique anchor exists. Here none does.
When Edit can't target a unique match, rewriting the whole file is the reliable fallback.

p.stem: Claude needs to find every caller of parseConfig across the codebase. Which tool fits best?
why: Searching file contents is how you find every call site.
Right for finding files by name. Callers are found by content.
Right for making an edit. This is a search.
Right for a non-unique edit. This is a search.

options: Hand off to a human when the customer explicitly asks for one.
Ask a clarifying question when the request matches more than one account.
Escalate when the request falls outside what the documented policy covers.
Resolve it directly when it's within policy, even if the customer is upset.

h.stem: A customer asks for compensation for a missed delivery date. The policy covers refunds for late deliveries but says nothing about compensation. What should the agent do?
why: Right when a person is requested. The customer hasn't asked for one.
Right when the account is unclear. Here the account is known; the policy has a gap.
When the policy doesn't cover a request, a person should decide rather than the agent improvising.
Right for in-policy requests. This one falls outside the policy.

p.stem: A customer signed “J. Smith” asks about “my order,” and the lookup returns three customers with that name. What should the agent do?
why: Right when a person is requested. Nobody asked for one.
With several matches, ask for an identifier instead of guessing.
Right for gaps in the policy. This is an identification problem.
Right for in-policy requests. First the agent needs to know whose order it is.

options: Keep a case-facts block with amounts, dates and order numbers, re-sent every turn.
Trim each tool result down to the few fields the agent actually uses.
Summarize the earlier part of the conversation once it gets long.
Place the key findings at the start of the input, not buried in the middle.

h.stem: Late in a 40-turn chat, the agent misquotes a refund amount agreed early on. The running summary it keeps says only “discussed a refund.” What fixes this?
why: Exact values need to be stored verbatim; summaries lose them.
Right when tool output bloats the context. Here a key value was lost.
That's the current approach, and it dropped the amount.
Right when long inputs bury findings. Here the value isn't in the input anymore.

p.stem: Each order lookup returns 40 fields, and the agent uses about 5 of them. Long chats hit the context limit. What fixes this?
why: Right for keeping exact facts. Here the problem is bloat.
Cut tool output to what matters, before it accumulates in the context.
Right for long conversational history. The bloat here is tool output.
Right when findings get lost in the middle. Here the problem is volume.

options: Delegate the exploration to a subagent and keep only its summary.
Have Claude write key findings to a scratchpad file it can reread later.
Run /compact once the session gets long.
Start a fresh session seeded with a summary of the decisions so far.

h.stem: Hours into a refactoring session, Claude starts referring to “typical patterns” instead of the specific classes it found earlier. It will need those exact findings for several more hours of work. What fits best?
why: Right before a big exploration. The findings already exist; they're fading.
Writing findings to a file preserves them exactly, beyond what the context holds.
Compaction summarizes, so the specific details it needs may be lost.
Right when earlier context is stale. Here it's accurate but fading.

p.stem: Before starting a feature, Claude must survey 200 files to find where configuration is loaded. The survey output would fill the session. What fits best?
why: A subagent explores in its own context and returns only what matters.
Right for preserving findings over a long session. The issue here is the volume of exploration.
Right once a session gets long. Here the overload hasn't happened yet.
Right when earlier context is stale. There's no earlier context here.

options: Grep for the symbol first and read only the files that match.
Have Claude record its findings in a scratchpad file as it goes.
Delegate the investigation to a subagent and keep only its summary.
Run /compact after the investigation to free up space.

h.stem: To fix one bug, Claude reads entire 3,000-line files one after another and runs out of context before it reaches the bug. What fits best?
why: Search narrowly first, and read only what's relevant.
Right for keeping findings across a long session. Here the reading is unfocused.
Right for a broad survey. This is a targeted bug hunt.
Right after a long investigation. It doesn't stop the wasteful reading.

p.stem: A developer wants a summary of how authentication works across 15 services, and wants the main session kept free for the implementation that follows. What fits best?
why: Right for a targeted search. This is a broad survey.
Right for preserving findings. The survey would still fill the main context.
A broad survey in a separate context returns only the summary.
Right once a session is long. It's better not to fill it in the first place.

options: Keep claim-to-source mappings through synthesis, with each source's date.
Report conflicting figures side by side with their sources instead of picking one.
Label which findings are well established and which are contested.
Have the synthesis agent re-check each claim against its cited source.

h.stem: Two recent, reputable studies report different adoption rates. The report silently averages them into one figure. What fits best?
why: Right when attribution is lost. Here the conflict is hidden.
Preserve the conflict, with attribution, so readers can see the disagreement.
Right for the report as a whole. Here a specific conflict needs showing.
Right when synthesis introduces errors. Both figures here are accurate.

p.stem: The final report states figures without any indication of where each came from, so editors can't check them. What fits best?
why: Carry the source, and its date, with every claim so it can be traced.
Right when sources disagree. Here attribution is missing.
Right for marking certainty. Editors still couldn't trace the figures.
Right when synthesis distorts claims. Here attribution is missing.

options: Store each value with its document, page and the quoted source text.
Keep both values and flag the conflict for review, instead of choosing one.
Record the document version and date alongside each extracted value.
Route low-confidence values to a person for review.

h.stem: Two invoices for the same order show different totals. The pipeline keeps whichever one it read last. What fits best?
why: Right when values can't be traced. Here two traceable values conflict.
Surface the conflict, with both values and their sources, instead of silently choosing.
Right when values change across versions. These are two different documents.
Right for uncertain values. Both values here were read clearly.

p.stem: Auditors ask where a figure in the summary came from, and nobody can tell without re-reading every document. What fits best?
why: Store provenance with each value so it can be traced instantly.
Right when values conflict. Here the problem is traceability.
Right when versions matter. The location still wouldn't be recorded.
Right for uncertain values. Here the problem is traceability.

options: Have the subagent retry transient errors locally before reporting.
Report the failure type, the query and any partial results to the coordinator.
Continue with the other subagents and mark the gap in the final report.
Distinguish “no results found” from “search failed” in what subagents return.

h.stem: One of five subagents fails for good, because its source is offline all day. The coordinator abandons the whole report. What fits best?
why: Right for brief, transient faults. This source is down all day.
Right when the coordinator lacks details. It already knows the source is down.
Deliver what the other four found, and say clearly what's missing.
Right when two kinds of result look the same. Here the failure is clear.

p.stem: A subagent returns “no relevant sources” both when a search found nothing and when the search API crashed, and the coordinator treats both the same way. What fits best?
why: Right for transient faults. The coordinator still can't tell the two cases apart.
Right for failure details. First the two outcomes must be told apart.
Right when a failure is known. Here failures are disguised as empty results.
An empty result and a failure need different handling, so they must look different.

options: Calibrate the confidence threshold on a labeled sample before relying on it.
Keep sampling high-confidence extractions for ongoing spot checks.
Route fields below the confidence threshold to human review.
Break accuracy down by document type and field, not just overall.

h.stem: Overall accuracy is 97%, so the team plans to stop human review entirely. Nobody has looked at accuracy by document type. What should happen first?
why: Right when confidence scores aren't yet tied to accuracy. The gap here is in how accuracy is measured.
Right after automation, to catch drift. First check what the 97% hides.
Right once thresholds are calibrated. First check where the errors are.
An overall rate can hide document types that fail badly.

p.stem: The model reports a confidence for each field. The team wants to route review by it, but nobody knows what 0.8 actually means for accuracy. What should happen first?
why: Measure how confidence relates to accuracy on labeled data before acting on it.
Right after routing is in place. First the scores need meaning.
That relies on the threshold before anyone knows what it means.
Right for finding weak segments. Here the confidence scale itself is unknown.
